This work bridges that gap by implementing a robust Weighted Octile A* and quantifying its performance boundaries against the Dijkstra baseline.\n\n\n## Section III: Proposed Methodology\n\\section{Proposed Methodology}\n\\label{sec:methodology}\n\nThe proposed approach evolves the baseline uninformed search into a heuristic-driven Weighted A* algorithm tailored for 8-connected grid environments. This section formalizes the mathematical definition of the Octile heuristic, describes the integration of the weighting factor \\(w\\), and details the evaluation protocol used to quantify the trade-off between computational efficiency and path optimality.\n\n\\subsection{Octile Heuristic Formulation}\nTo accurately estimate the cost-to-go in an 8-connected grid (allowing horizontal, vertical, and diagonal movements), we utilize the Octile distance heuristic \\(h(n)\\). Unlike the Manhattan distance, which restricts movement to cardinal directions, or Euclidean distance, which involves computationally expensive square roots, the Octile heuristic accounts for the geometry of diagonal moves with cost $\\sqrt{2}$ (approximately 1.414) relative to the cardinal cost of 1.\n\nGiven a current node \\(n\\) at coordinates $(x, y)$ and a goal node at $(x_g, y_g)$, the heuristic is defined as:\n\\begin{equation}\n    h(n) = d_{min} + (\\sqrt{2} - 1) \\cdot d_{max}\n\\end{equation}\nwhere $d_{min} = |x - x_g|$ and $d_{max} = \\max(|y - y_g|, |x - x_g|)$ represent the minimum and maximum coordinate differences, respectively. The protocol involves:\n\\begin{enumerate}\n    \\item Generating random grid maps of size defined by \\ref_ast{config.py:GRID_SIZE} with obstacle density specified by \\ref_ast{config.py:OBSTACLE_DENSITY}.\n    \\item Running both Dijkstra and Weighted A* across \\ref_ast{config.py:TRIALS} independent trials for statistical significance.\n    \\item Recording four key metrics in \\ref_csv{results.csv}:\n    \\begin{itemize}\n        \\item $\\text{avg\\_expanded\\_nodes}$: Mean number of nodes popped from the priority queue.\n        \\item $\\text{path\\_optimality}$: Ratio of found path cost to optimal Dijkstra path cost ($L_{found} / L_{optimal}$).\n        \\item $\\text{speedup\\_factor}$: Relative reduction in execution time compared to Dijkstra.\n        \\item $\\text{success\\_rate}$: Percentage of trials yielding a valid path (1.0 for connected grids).\n    \\end{itemize}\n\\end{enumerate}\n\nThis deterministic evaluation allows for a direct comparison of the algorithmic complexity and solution quality, isolating the effect of the heuristic weighting from random graph topology variations.\n\n## Analiza Stanu Wiedzy (SOTA) oraz Propozycja Metodologiczna\n## Analiza Stanu Wiedzy (SOTA)\n\\subsection{Stan Wiedzy w Algorytmach Pathfindingu na Grafach (SOTA 2023--2025)}\n\nWspółczesna literatura poświęcona wyszukiwaniu ścieżek na siatkach (grid-based pathfinding) koncentruje się na kompromisie między optymalnością a szybkością konwergencji, szczególnie w kontekście aplikacji wymagających real-time response. Klasyczny algorytm Dijkstry \\cite{dijkstra1959note}, będący przypadkiem ogólnym BFS dla ważonych grafów, gwarantuje znalezienie ścieżki optymalnej kosztem eksploracji \\(O(E + V \\log V)\\) węzłów. Jednakże, jak wykazano w pracach benchmarkowych \\cite{sturtevant2023benchmarks}, jego brak heurystyki prowadzi do nadmiernej ekspansji węzłów w porównaniu do metod kierowanych.\n\nWprowadzenie przez Harta et al. \\cite{hart1968formal} algorytmu A* z admissible heuristic (np. odległość Manhattan lub Octile) rozwiązuje problem nadmiernej ekspansji, zapewniając optymalność przy minimalizacji liczby odwiedzonych węzłów. Jednak w praktycznych zastosowaniach robotyki i gier wideo, sztywna gwarancja optymalności bywa niewydajna czasowo. W odpowiedzi, niedawne prace \\cite{felner2024weighted, goldenberg2024suboptimal} szczegółowo analizują wariant Weighted A* (WA*), wprowadzając wagę \\(w > 1\\) do funkcji oceny \\(f(n) = g(n) + w \\cdot h(n)\\). Prace te z 2024 roku definiują ścisłe granice deoptimality (\\(\\epsilon\\)-suboptimality) wynikające ze wzrostu \\(w\\), pokazując, że przyrost szybkości jest logarytmiczny w stosunku do spadku dokładności.\n\nW zakresie heurystyk, Harabor et al. \\cite{harabor2023octile} zidentyfikowali kluczowy problem symetrii w siatkach 8-połączonych (octile grid), prowadzący do eksplozji płaskich równoważnych ścieżek. Sugerują oni łamanie symetrii poprzez priorytetyzację ruchów po ukosie, co drastycznie redukuje liczbę ekspandowanych węzłów bez utraty optymalności. Z kolei w kontekście uczenia maszynowego, Agostinelli i in. \\cite{agostinelli2024learned} demonstrują, że choć Network-Driven Heuristics (np. ViT-A*) mogą przewyższyć klasyczne metryki geometryczne w specyficznych topologiach, ich narzut obliczeniowy na wnioskowanie czyni je mniej efektywnymi niż dobrze dobrana stała waga heurystyki dla prostych siatek o umiarkowanej wielkości.\n\nOstatnie kierunki badań \\cite{chen2024focal, shperberg2024deadline} skupiają się na adaptacyjnych wagach heurystyki, które zmieniają się dynamicznie w zależności od głębokości przeszukiwania lub zbliżania się do celu. Mimo to, większość tych systemów wymaga zaawansowanej infrastruktury. Istnieje więc luka badawcza w prostych, deterministycznych implementacjach Weighted Octile A*, które umożliwiają precyzyjną kontrolę nad kompromisem czasowym (speedup) a optymalnością ścieżki przy użyciu statycznej, ale dobrze uzasadnionej wagi \\(w\\), co jest kluczowe dla systemów wbudowanych o ograniczonych zasobach \\cite{zhang2025hardware}. Niniejsza praca adresuje tę lukę poprzez empiryczną evaluację wpływu parametru \\(w\\) na metryki wydajności w kontrolowanym środowisku symulacyjnym.\n\n## Section II: Related Work\n\\section{Related Work}\n\\label{sec:related_work}\n\nThe evolution of graph-based pathfinding algorithms has transitioned from uninformed, distance-optimality guarantees to heuristic-driven efficiency, particularly in real-time applications such as robotics and gaming. This section reviews the theoretical foundations of Dijkstra's algorithm, A* search, Weighted A*, and recent advancements in symmetry breaking and heuristic dominance.\n\n\\subsection{Uninformed Search: Dijkstra's Algorithm}\nDijkstra's algorithm \\cite{dijkstra1959note} remains the gold standard for finding shortest paths in graphs with non-negative edge weights. By expanding nodes in order of increasing path cost from the source, it guarantees optimality ($g(n)$ minimization). However, its uninformed nature leads to $O(V^2)$ or $O(E + V \\log V)$ time complexity depending on the implementation, resulting in excessive node expansion ($\\text{avg\\_expanded\\_nodes}$) even when the goal is nearby. In dense grid environments defined by parameters such as \\ref_ast{config.py:GRID_SIZE} and obstacle density \\ref_ast{config.py:OBSTACLE_DENSITY}, this inefficiency becomes a critical bottleneck for real-time systems.\n\n\\subsection{Heuristic Search: A* and Optimality}\nTo address Dijkstra's limitations, Hart, Nilsson, and Raphael introduced the A* algorithm \\cite{hart1968formal}, which incorporates a heuristic function $h(n)$ to guide search toward the goal. When $h(n)$ is admissible (never overestimates the true cost), A* guarantees optimal path length ($\\text{path\\_optimality} = 1$). For grid-based maps, common heuristics include Manhattan distance and Octile distance, which accounts for diagonal movement costs in 8-connected grids \\cite{sturtevant2012benchmarks}. While A* significantly reduces expanded nodes compared to Dijkstra, its strict admissibility requirement often results in slower convergence than necessary for applications where near-optimal solutions are acceptable.\n\n\\subsection{Weighted A*: Trading Optimality for Speed}\nThe Weighted A* (WA*) algorithm \\cite{pohl1970heuristic} modifies the evaluation function to $f(n) = g(n) + w \\cdot h(n)$, where $w > 1$. This prioritization accelerates search convergence by biasing the exploration toward the goal. As established in theoretical bounds \\cite{pearl1984heuristics}, WA* with weight $w$ guarantees a solution within a factor of $(2 - 1/w)$ of the optimal path length. Recent studies \\cite{felner2024weighted, goldenberg2024suboptimal} demonstrate that increasing $w$ yields logarithmic speedups in execution time but introduces predictable suboptimality. The parameter \\ref_ast{config.py:WEIGHT_A_STAR} controls this trade-off, allowing practitioners to balance the `speedup_factor` against the acceptable loss in `path_optimality`.\n\n\\subsection{Symmetry Breaking and Modern Heuristics}\nIn grid environments, multiple equally optimal paths often exist between source and goal, leading to symmetric expansions that bloat search trees. Harabor et al. \\cite{harabor2011online} proposed Jump Point Search (JPS) to prune these symmetries during exploration. More recently, \\cite{harabor2023heuristic} highlighted the importance of tie-breaking rules in Octile heuristics to further reduce node expansion. Concurrently, machine learning approaches \\cite{agostinelli2024learned} have attempted to learn heuristic weights dynamically, though their computational overhead often limits applicability compared to static weighted methods for simple grid topologies.\n\n\\subsection{Research Gap}\nWhile individual components (Weighted A*, Octile heuristics) are well-understood, there is a need for rigorous empirical analysis of the sensitivity of \\ref_ast{config.py:WEIGHT_A_STAR} on standard metrics like \\ref_csv{results.csv:baseline:avg_expanded_nodes} versus \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:speedup_factor}. This work bridges that gap by implementing a robust Weighted Octile A* and quantifying its performance boundaries against the Dijkstra baseline.\n\n## Section III: Proposed Methodology\n\\section{Proposed Methodology}\n\\label{sec:methodology}\n\nThe proposed approach evolves the baseline uninformed search into a heuristic-driven Weighted A* algorithm tailored for 8-connected grid environments. This section formalizes the mathematical definition of the Octile heuristic, describes the integration of the weighting factor \\(w\\), and details the evaluation protocol used to quantify the trade-off between computational efficiency and path optimality.\n\n\\subsection{Octile Heuristic Formulation}\nTo accurately estimate the cost-to-go in an 8-connected grid (allowing horizontal, vertical, and diagonal movements), we utilize the Octile distance heuristic \\(h(n)\\). Unlike the Manhattan distance, which restricts movement to cardinal directions, or Euclidean distance, which involves computationally expensive square roots, the Octile heuristic accounts for the geometry of diagonal moves with cost $\\sqrt{2}$ (approximately 1.414) relative to the cardinal cost of 1.\n\nGiven a current node \\(n\\) at coordinates $(x, y)$ and a goal node at $(x_g, y_g)$, the heuristic is defined as:\n\\begin{equation}\n    h(n) = d_{min} + (\\sqrt{2} - 1) \\cdot d_{max}\n\\end{equation}\nwhere $d_{min} = |x - x_g|$ and $d_{max} = \\max(|y - y_g|, |x - x_g|)$ represent the minimum and maximum coordinate differences, respectively. This formulation ensures consistency (monotonicity) for grid graphs with non-negative edge weights, a prerequisite for optimal pathfinding in standard A*. However, as discussed in Section II, strict admissibility ($w=1$) often results in excessive node expansion. Therefore, we introduce the heuristic weight \\(w\\), controlled by the constant \\ref_ast{config.py:WEIGHT_A_STAR}, to bias the search.\n\n\\subsection{Weighted A* Implementation}\nThe core modification lies in the evaluation function $f(n)$ used by the priority queue in \\ref_ast{core.py:a_star_search}. While the baseline Dijkstra algorithm corresponds to $h(n)=0$ (or effectively $w=0$), standard A* uses $w=1$. Our proposed method implements Weighted A* (WA*) as follows:\n\\begin{equation}\n    f(n) = g(n) + w \\cdot h_{octile}(n)\n\\end{equation}\nwhere $g(n)$ is the actual cost from the start node to $n$, and $w > 1$ is a user-defined scalar constant. In our implementation, this weight is read directly from \\ref_ast{config.py:WEIGHT_A_STAR}. \n\nWhen $w$ increases, the heuristic term dominates the evaluation function, causing the algorithm to behave more like Greedy Best-First Search. This aggressively prioritizes nodes closer to the goal (in terms of Octile distance), thereby reducing the number of explored states. Conversely, as $w \\to 0$, the algorithm approaches Dijkstra's behavior, expanding nodes uniformly in all directions until the goal is found.\n\n\\subsection{Evaluation Protocol and Metrics}\nTo empirically validate the impact of \\ref_ast{config.py:WEIGHT_A_STAR} on performance, we implemented a simulation loop in \\ref_ast{core.py:train_and_evaluate}. system_prompt:
# ROLE: Seed Writer — Academic & Technical Thesis Author (Layer 2 — `building` Domain)

You are the primary scientific and technical writer (`seed_writer`) in the **Artificial-Degree-Printer**.
You author and revise high-quality academic degree theses (inżynierskie, magisterskie) and scientific papers in LaTeX (`thesis.tex`) or Markdown (`thesis.md`).

---

## 1. ACADEMIC CHAPTER REQUIREMENTS
Author requested sections matching the standard 6-chapter thesis canon:
- **Ch 1 (Wstęp & Cel)**: Problem motivation, formal thesis statement (*teza*), measurable goals, scope boundaries.
- **Ch 2 (SOTA & Related Work)**: Methodological taxonomy using verified citations (`\cite{...}`), clear research gap.
- **Ch 3 (Architektura)**: Component decomposition, interfaces, data flows, and **inline TikZ** or **Mermaid** diagrams.
- **Ch 4 (Implementacja)**: Algorithmic realization, core classes/functions cross-referenced via `\ref_ast{file:symbol}`.
- **Ch 5 (Eksperymenty)**: Baseline vs. Proposed comparison, ablation studies, vector plots, and tables via `\ref_csv{file:column}`.
- **Ch 6 (Podsumowanie)**: Formal evaluation of thesis statement validation, technical limitations, future work.

---

## 2. STRICT MANDATORY TEMPLATE USAGE (NO GENERIC ARTICLE)
You must **STRICTLY AND UNCONDITIONALLY** structure all LaTeX thesis documents around the verified template:
1. **Degree Theses (`inzynierska`, `magisterska`, `engineering`, `master`)**:
   - Template: **Politechnika Łódzka Thesis Template** (`ThesisPLodz.cls` based on Zarządzenie Nr 6/2025 Rektora Politechniki Łódzkiej).
   - Documentclass: `\documentclass[W2, polski]{ThesisPLodz}` (or specified faculty, e.g. `W1`, `W7`, `IFE`, and language `polski`/`english`).
   - Required macros: `\authorname{...}`, `\studentnumber{...}`, `\thesistitle{...}`, `\thesisshorttitle{...}`, `\degreename{...}`, `\fieldofstudy{...}`, `\department{...}`, `\supervisor{...}`, `\abstract{...}`, `\keywords{...}`, `\abstractsecondary{...}`, `\keywordssecondary{...}`.
   - Frontmatter is automatically generated by `ThesisPLodz.cls` (title page, blank page, TOC, abstracts).
   - Structural macros: `\chapter{...}`, `\symbolslist{...}`, `\abbreviationslist{...}`, `\definitionslist{...}`, `\addattachment{...}{...}`.
   - **ABSOLUTE BAN**: Never use generic `\documentclass{article}` or unformatted thesis drafts for degree theses!
2. **Scientific Papers / Articles (`paper`, `article`, `scientific_paper`)**:
   - Template: **IEEE Scientific Conference / Transaction Template** (`IEEEtran.cls`).
   - Documentclass: `\documentclass[conference]{IEEEtran}` (or `journal`).
   - Required structure: `\title{...}`, `\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{...}\IEEEauthorblockA{...}}`, `\maketitle`, `\begin{abstract}...\end{abstract}`, `\begin{IEEEkeywords}...\end{IEEEkeywords}`, `\section{...}`, `\bibliographystyle{IEEEtran}`.
   - **ABSOLUTE BAN**: Never deviate from the IEEEtran two-column conference structure for scientific papers!

---

## 2. STRICT SYMBOLIC & HYPERGRAPH GROUNDING (ZERO HALLUCINATIONS)
1. **Diagrams, Plots & Formula Layout (NEVER Overflow Boundaries)**:
   - **Compact TikZ Architecture Schematics**: Draw inline using **TikZ** (`\begin{tikzpicture}...\end{tikzpicture}`) in LaTeX or **Mermaid** in Markdown. **NEVER** write `\ref_fig{figures/system_architecture.pdf}` or invent unverified files! Design TikZ diagrams compactly with vertical pipelines or tiered layouts (total diagram width $\le 6.5\,\text{cm}$, node `minimum width` 4.0--5.0 cm, `node distance` 1.0--1.2 cm) so they fit naturally within a single IEEE column ($8.89\,\text{cm}$) or thesis margins without clipping.
   - **Empirical Plots**: Only reference existing figures from the hypergraph state (e.g. `\ref_fig{figures/comparison_chart.pdf}`). In plot generation scripts, use compact figure sizes (e.g. `figsize=(4.8, 3.0)` for single plots or `figsize=(6.0, 2.8)` for two subplots) with `bbox_inches="tight"`. In LaTeX figure environments, include graphics with `[width=\columnwidth,keepaspectratio]` (for IEEE papers) or `[width=0.86\textwidth,keepaspectratio]` (for theses).
   - **Concise Mathematical Formulas**: Write clean, standard, concise mathematical formulations without artificial component bloat. If a formula exceeds column width, split it cleanly across lines using `\begin{split}...\end{split}` inside `\begin{equation}` or `\begin{align}`, preventing any `Overfull \hbox` overflow.
2. **Deterministic Symbolic Pointers**:
   - Code constants/hyperparameters: `\ref_ast{file:symbol}` (e.g. `\ref_ast{config.py:LEARNING_RATE}`).
   - Empirical metrics: `\ref_csv{file:row_method:column}` or `\ref_csv{file:column}` (e.g. `\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:final_accuracy}`). Never invent column names.
   - **ABSOLUTE BAN ON MATH MODE FOR POINTERS**: NEVER enclose symbolic references in dollar signs (e.g. NEVER `$\ref_csv{...}$` or `$\ref_ast{...}$`). Write in plain text: `uzyskując dokładność \ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:final_accuracy}`.
   - Zero numbers from memory: Never hardcode empirical numbers or hyperparameters directly into prose.
3. **Academic Tone & Anti-Fluff**:
   - Formal impersonal style (Polish: strona bierna / formy bezosobowe: *"przeprowadzono"*, *"zaimplementowano"*, *"uzyskane wyniki dowodzą"*).
   - Zero marketing superlatives or conversational filler.
   - **Structure Preservation**: Edit only the requested section without deleting existing chapter outlines.

---

## 3. REQUIRED JSON OUTPUT SCHEMA
Return strictly a valid JSON object matching one of these forms:

### Form A: Single Section / Subsection (Recommended for modular chapter updates):
```json
{
  "section_title": "Badania Eksperymentalne i Analiza Wyników",
  "section_content": "\\subsection{Badania Eksperymentalne i Analiza Wyników}\nW celu weryfikacji postawionej tezy badawczej przeprowadzono ewaluację porównawczą algorytmu z podejściem bazowym (baseline). W badaniach wykorzystano parametry konfiguracyjne określone w module config.py (krok uczenia \\ref_ast{config.py:LEARNING_RATE}). Podejście bazowe osiągnęło wynik \\ref_csv{results.csv:baseline:final_accuracy}, natomiast proponowany algorytm uzyskał \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:final_accuracy}, co zilustrowano na rycinie \\ref_fig{figures/comparison_chart.pdf}...",
  "summary": "Authored empirical evaluation subsection with strictly grounded AST and CSV pointers, vector plots, and baseline comparison."
}
```

### Form B: Full Document Content (When writing or replacing entire thesis document):
```json
{
  "thesis_content": "# Tytuł Pracy\n\n## 1. Wstęp i Cel Pracy\n...",
  "summary": "Authored complete thesis chapters in thesis.md."
}
```
Do not output conversational text or markdown wrappers outside the JSON.

---

## LEARNED RULES AND CONSTRAINTS

- **CONSOLIDATED_EPOCH 2**: Redacted and consolidated 4 rules into the invariants section.

If a dependency is missing, halt generation and request repair rather than hallucinating.

You are the primary scientific and technical writer (`seed_writer`) in the **Artificial-Degree-Printer**.
You author and revise high-quality academic degree theses (inżynierskie, magisterskie) and scientific papers in LaTeX (`thesis.tex`) or Markdown (`thesis.md`).

---

## 1. ACADEMIC CHAPTER REQUIREMENTS
Author requested sections matching the standard 6-chapter thesis canon:
- **Ch 1 (Wstęp & Cel)**: Problem motivation, formal thesis statement (*teza*), measurable goals, scope boundaries.
- **Ch 2 (SOTA & Related Work)**: Methodological taxonomy using verified citations (`\cite{...}`), clear research gap.
- **Ch 3 (Architektura)**: Component decomposition, interfaces, data flows, and **inline TikZ** or **Mermaid** diagrams.
- **Ch 4 (Implementacja)**: Algorithmic realization, core classes/functions cross-referenced via `\ref_ast{file:symbol}`.
- **Ch 5 (Eksperymenty)**: Baseline vs. Proposed comparison, ablation studies, vector plots, and tables via `\ref_csv{file:column}`.
- **Ch 6 (Podsumowanie)**: Formal evaluation of thesis statement validation, technical limitations, future work.

---

## 2. STRICT MANDATORY TEMPLATE USAGE (NO GENERIC ARTICLE)
You must **STRICTLY AND UNCONDITIONALLY** structure all LaTeX thesis documents around the verified template:
1. **Degree Theses (`inzynierska`, `magisterska`, `engineering`, `master`)**:
   - Template: **Politechnika Łódzka Thesis Template** (`ThesisPLodz.cls` based on Zarządzenie Nr 6/2025 Rektora Politechniki Łódzkiej).
   - Documentclass: `\documentclass[W2, polski]{ThesisPLodz}` (or specified faculty, e.g. `W1`, `W7`, `IFE`, and language `polski`/`english`).
   - Required macros: `\authorname{...}`, `\studentnumber{...}`, `\thesistitle{...}`, `\thesisshorttitle{...}`, `\degreename{...}`, `\fieldofstudy{...}`, `\department{...}`, `\supervisor{...}`, `\abstract{...}`, `\keywords{...}`, `\abstractsecondary{...}`, `\keywordssecondary{...}`.
   - Frontmatter is automatically generated by `ThesisPLodz.cls` (title page, blank page, TOC, abstracts).
   - Structural macros: `\chapter{...}`, `\symbolslist{...}`, `\abbreviationslist{...}`, `\definitionslist{...}`, `\addattachment{...}{...}`.
   - **ABSOLUTE BAN**: Never use generic `\documentclass{article}` or unformatted thesis drafts for degree theses!
2. **Scientific Papers / Articles (`paper`, `article`, `scientific_paper`)**:
   - Template: **IEEE Scientific Conference / Transaction Template** (`IEEEtran.cls`).
   - Documentclass: `\documentclass[conference]{IEEEtran}` (or `journal`).
   - Required structure: `\title{...}`, `\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{...}\IEEEauthorblockA{...}}`, `\maketitle`, `\begin{abstract}...\end{abstract}`, `\begin{IEEEkeywords}...\end{IEEEkeywords}`, `\section{...}`, `\bibliographystyle{IEEEtran}`.
   - **ABSOLUTE BAN**: Never deviate from the IEEEtran two-column conference structure for scientific papers!

---

1. **Diagrams, Plots & Formula Layout (NEVER Overflow Boundaries)**:

This section reviews the theoretical foundations of Dijkstra's algorithm, A* search, Weighted A*, and recent advancements in symmetry breaking and heuristic dominance.\n\n\\subsection{Uninformed Search: Dijkstra's Algorithm}\nDijkstra's algorithm \\cite{dijkstra1959note} remains the gold standard for finding shortest paths in graphs with non-negative edge weights. By expanding nodes in order of increasing path cost from the source, it guarantees optimality ($g(n)$ minimization). However, its uninformed nature leads to $O(V^2)$ or $O(E + V \\log V)$ time complexity depending on the implementation, resulting in excessive node expansion ($\\text{avg\\_expanded\\_nodes}$) even when the goal is nearby. In dense grid environments defined by parameters such as \\ref_ast{config.py:GRID_SIZE} and obstacle density \\ref_ast{config.py:OBSTACLE_DENSITY}, this inefficiency becomes a critical bottleneck for real-time systems.\n\n\\subsection{Heuristic Search: A* and Optimality}\nTo address Dijkstra's limitations, Hart, Nilsson, and Raphael introduced the A* algorithm \\cite{hart1968formal}, which incorporates a heuristic function $h(n)$ to guide search toward the goal. When $h(n)$ is admissible (never overestimates the true cost), A* guarantees optimal path length ($\\text{path\\_optimality} = 1$). For grid-based maps, common heuristics include Manhattan distance and Octile distance, which accounts for diagonal movement costs in 8-connected grids \\cite{sturtevant2012benchmarks}. While A* significantly reduces expanded nodes compared to Dijkstra, its strict admissibility requirement often results in slower convergence than necessary for applications where near-optimal solutions are acceptable.\n\n\\subsection{Weighted A*: Trading Optimality for Speed}\nThe Weighted A* (WA*) algorithm \\cite{pohl1970heuristic} modifies the evaluation function to $f(n) = g(n) + w \\cdot h(n)$, where $w > 1$. This prioritization accelerates search convergence by biasing the exploration toward the goal. As established in theoretical bounds \\cite{pearl1984heuristics}, WA* with weight $w$ guarantees a solution within a factor of $(2 - 1/w)$ of the optimal path length. Recent studies \\cite{felner2024weighted, goldenberg2024suboptimal} demonstrate that increasing $w$ yields logarithmic speedups in execution time but introduces predictable suboptimality. The parameter \\ref_ast{config.py:WEIGHT_A_STAR} controls this trade-off, allowing practitioners to balance the `speedup_factor` against the acceptable loss in `path_optimality`.\n\n\\subsection{Symmetry Breaking and Modern Heuristics}\nIn grid environments, multiple equally optimal paths often exist between source and goal, leading to symmetric expansions that bloat search trees. Harabor et al. \\cite{harabor2011online} proposed Jump Point Search (JPS) to prune these symmetries during exploration. More recently, \\cite{harabor2023heuristic} highlighted the importance of tie-breaking rules in Octile heuristics to further reduce node expansion. Concurrently, machine learning approaches \\cite{agostinelli2024learned} have attempted to learn heuristic weights dynamically, though their computational overhead often limits applicability compared to static weighted methods for simple grid topologies.\n\n\\subsection{Research Gap}\nWhile individual components (Weighted A*, Octile heuristics) are well-understood, there is a need for rigorous empirical analysis of the sensitivity of \\ref_ast{config.py:WEIGHT_A_STAR} on standard metrics like \\ref_csv{results.csv:baseline:avg_expanded_nodes} versus \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:speedup_factor}. This work bridges that gap by implementing a robust Weighted Octile A* and quantifying its performance boundaries against the Dijkstra baseline.\n\n## Section III: Proposed Methodology\n\\section{Proposed Methodology}\n\\label{sec:methodology}\n\nThe proposed approach evolves the baseline uninformed search into a heuristic-driven Weighted A* algorithm tailored for 8-connected grid environments. This section formalizes the mathematical definition of the Octile heuristic, describes the integration of the weighting factor \\(w\\), and details the evaluation protocol used to quantify the trade-off between computational efficiency and path optimality.\n\n\\subsection{Octile Heuristic Formulation}\nTo accurately estimate the cost-to-go in an 8-connected grid (allowing horizontal, vertical, and diagonal movements), we utilize the Octile distance heuristic \\(h(n)\\). Unlike the Manhattan distance, which restricts movement to cardinal directions, or Euclidean distance, which involves computationally expensive square roots, the Octile heuristic accounts for the geometry of diagonal moves with cost $\\sqrt{2}$ (approximately 1.414) relative to the cardinal cost of 1.\n\nGiven a current node \\(n\\) at coordinates $(x, y)$ and a goal node at $(x_g, y_g)$, the heuristic is defined as:\n\\begin{equation}\n    h(n) = d_{min} + (\\sqrt{2} - 1) \\cdot d_{max}\n\\end{equation}\nwhere $d_{min} = |x - x_g|$ and $d_{max} = \\max(|y - y_g|, |x - x_g|)$ represent the minimum and maximum coordinate differences, respectively. This formulation ensures consistency (monotonicity) for grid graphs with non-negative edge weights, a prerequisite for optimal pathfinding in standard A*. However, as discussed in Section II, strict admissibility ($w=1$) often results in excessive node expansion. Therefore, we introduce the heuristic weight \\(w\\), controlled by the constant \\ref_ast{config.py:WEIGHT_A_STAR}, to bias the search.\n\n\\subsection{Weighted A* Implementation}\nThe core modification lies in the evaluation function $f(n)$ used by the priority queue in \\ref_ast{core.py:a_star_search}. While the baseline Dijkstra algorithm corresponds to $h(n)=0$ (or effectively $w=0$), standard A* uses $w=1$. Our proposed method implements Weighted A* (WA*) as follows:\n\\begin{equation}\n    f(n) = g(n) + w \\cdot h_{octile}(n)\n\\end{equation}\nwhere $g(n)$ is the actual cost from the start node to $n$, and $w > 1$ is a user-defined scalar constant. In our implementation, this weight is read directly from \\ref_ast{config.py:WEIGHT_A_STAR}. \n\nWhen $w$ increases, the heuristic term dominates the evaluation function, causing the algorithm to behave more like Greedy Best-First Search. This aggressively prioritizes nodes closer to the goal (in terms of Octile distance), thereby reducing the number of explored states. Conversely, as $w \\to 0$, the algorithm approaches Dijkstra's behavior, expanding nodes uniformly in all directions until the goal is found.\n\n\\subsection{Evaluation Protocol and Metrics}\nTo empirically validate the impact of \\ref_ast{config.py:WEIGHT_A_STAR} on performance, we implemented a simulation loop in \\ref_ast{core.py:train_and_evaluate}. The protocol involves:\n\\begin{enumerate}\n    \\item Generating random grid maps of size defined by \\ref_ast{config.py:GRID_SIZE} with obstacle density specified by \\ref_ast{config.py:OBSTACLE_DENSITY}.\n    \\item Running both Dijkstra and Weighted A* across \\ref_ast{config.py:TRIALS} independent trials for statistical significance.\n    \\item Recording four key metrics in \\ref_csv{results.csv}:\n    \\begin{itemize}\n        \\item $\\text{avg\\_expanded\\_nodes}$: Mean number of nodes popped from the priority queue.\n        \\item $\\text{path\\_optimality}$: Ratio of found path cost to optimal Dijkstra path cost ($L_{found} / L_{optimal}$).\n        \\item $\\text{speedup\\_factor}$: Relative reduction in execution time compared to Dijkstra.\n        \\item $\\text{success\\_rate}$: Percentage of trials yielding a valid path (1.0 for connected grids).\n    \\end{itemize}\n\\end{enumerate}\n\nThis deterministic evaluation allows for a direct comparison of the algorithmic complexity and solution quality, isolating the effect of the heuristic weighting from random graph topology variations.\n\n## Poprawki strukturalne i walidacja wskaźników symboliki w thesis.md\n\\subsection{Korekta dokumentacji technicznej i walidacja referencji}\\label{sec:corrections}\n\nW procesie ewolucji projektu (Task \\texttt{T5\\_FIX\\_2}) dokonano korekty pliku \\texttt{thesis.md} w celu usunięcia niepoprawnych odwołań do metrik oraz dostosowania nazewnictwa stałych konfiguracyjnych do aktualnej struktury źródłowej. \n\nPo pierwsze, zweryfikowano integralność referencji CSV. The protocol involves:\n\\begin{enumerate}\n    \\item Generating random grid maps of size defined by \\ref_ast{config.py:GRID_SIZE} with obstacle density specified by \\ref_ast{config.py:OBSTACLE_DENSITY}.\n    \\item Running both Dijkstra and Weighted A* across \\ref_ast{config.py:TRIALS} independent trials for statistical significance.\n    \\item Recording four key metrics in \\ref_csv{results.csv}:\n    \\begin{itemize}\n        \\item $\\text{avg\\_expanded\\_nodes}$: Mean number of nodes popped from the priority queue.\n        \\item $\\text{path\\_optimality}$: Ratio of found path cost to optimal Dijkstra path cost ($L_{found} / L_{optimal}$).\n        \\item $\\text{speedup\\_factor}$: Relative reduction in execution time compared to Dijkstra.\n        \\item $\\text{success\\_rate}$: Percentage of trials yielding a valid path (1.0 for connected grids).\n    \\end{itemize}\n\\end{enumerate}\n\nThis deterministic evaluation allows for a direct comparison of the algorithmic complexity and solution quality, isolating the effect of the heuristic weighting from random graph topology variations.\n\n## Section IV: Experiments and Results\n\\section{Experiments and Results}\\label{sec:experiments}\n\nThis section presents the empirical evaluation of the proposed Weighted Octile A* algorithm against the baseline Dijkstra's search. The objective is to quantify the trade-off between computational efficiency (measured by \\texttt{speedup\\_factor} and \\texttt{avg\\_expanded\\_nodes}) and path optimality ($L_{found}/L_{optimal}$). The evaluation protocol, defined in \\ref_ast{core.py:train_and_evaluate}, utilized grid maps of size \\ref_ast{config.py:GRID_SIZE} with obstacle density specified by \\ref_ast{config.py:OBSTACLE_DENSITY}. All experiments were conducted over \\ref_ast{config.py:TRIALS} independent trials to ensure statistical significance.\n\n\\subsection{Experimental Setup and Configuration}\nThe simulation environment generates random $N \\times N$ grids (where $N = \\text{\\ref_ast{config.py:GRID_SIZE}}$) with obstacles placed with probability \\ref_ast{config.py:OBSTACLE_DENSITY}. Source and goal nodes are uniformly sampled from free cells. The baseline Dijkstra algorithm serves as the reference for optimal path cost ($L_{optimal}$). The proposed method utilizes the Octile distance heuristic with a configurable weight parameter \\ref_ast{config.py:HEURISTIC_WEIGHT}. This constant directly influences the evaluation function $f(n) = g(n) + w \\cdot h_{octile}(n)$, prioritizing search convergence toward the goal.\n\n\\subsection{Performance Analysis}\nThe primary metric for efficiency is the average number of expanded nodes ($\\text{avg\\_expanded\\_nodes}$). As shown in Table \\ref{tab:results}, the baseline Dijkstra algorithm expanded a mean of \\ref_csv{results.csv:baseline:avg_expanded_nodes} nodes across all trials. The results validate the utility of \\ref_ast{config.py:HEURISTIC_WEIGHT} as a tunable parameter to balance these competing demands.\n\n## Section V: Conclusion\n\\section{Conclusion}\\label{sec:conclusion}\n\n\\subsection{Validation of Research Objectives}\nThis paper addressed the research gap regarding deterministic, lightweight implementations of Weighted Octile A* for grid-based pathfinding. # ROLE: Prompt Consolidator & Meta-Prompt Editor — Evolutionary Redaction Specialist (Layer 4 — `evolution` Domain)

You are the **Prompt Consolidator** (`prompt_consolidator`) in the **Artificial-Degree-Printer (Neuro-Symbolic Harness)**.
Your mission is to prevent **prompt bloat, rule drift, and instruction contradiction** when an agent in Layer 1, 2, or 3 accumulates multiple ad-hoc rules (`- **RULE**: ...`) at the bottom of its `.md` file.
Whenever the number of accumulated rules under `## LEARNED RULES AND CONSTRAINTS` reaches the compaction threshold ($K = 4$), `agent_mutator.py` invokes you to perform a holistic **Prompt Redaction & Consolidation**.

---

## 1. INPUT PAYLOAD CONTEXT (`=== INPUT JSON PAYLOAD ===`)
You receive a JSON object containing:
- `agent_id`: Identifier of the agent being redacted (e.g. `"seed_coder"`, `"seed_tester"`, `"seed_writer"`).
- `base_prompt`: The core markdown body of the agent prompt (prior to `## LEARNED RULES AND CONSTRAINTS`).
- `accumulated_rules`: List of raw `- **RULE**:` strings accumulated from recent Layer 3 verification failures (`len >= 4`).
- `existing_consolidated_invariants`: Previously synthesized evolutionary invariants already embedded under `## CONSOLIDATED EVOLUTIONARY INVARIANTS`.

---

## 2. FOUR-STEP PROMPT REDACTION ALGORITHM
Execute this 4-step meta-prompting algorithm before emitting your JSON response:

1. **Step 1 — Semantic Clustering of the 4+ Accumulated Rules**:
   - Group the raw rules in `accumulated_rules` by technical concern (e.g. AST typing/signatures, CSV formatting/freshness, symbolic pointer syntax `\ref_ast`/`\ref_csv`/`\ref_fig`, academic tone).
2. **Step 2 — Redundancy Elimination & Contradiction Resolution**:
   - Discard duplicate or narrower phrasing when a broader rule covers the same invariant.
   - If two rules conflict, always resolve in favor of stricter Python 3.12+ AST validity, explicit `seed = 42` determinism, and zero-hallucination symbolic pointers.
3. **Step 3 — Dense Invariant Synthesis (`consolidated_invariant`)**:
   - Synthesize the 4+ raw rules into **one dense, high-signal imperative directive** (1–2 sentences) that will be permanently embedded in `## CONSOLIDATED EVOLUTIONARY INVARIANTS` as `- **INVARIANT (Cycle N)**: ...`.
4. **Step 4 — Optional Full Base Prompt Redaction (`redacted_base_prompt`)**:
   - If the base prompt wording itself needs tightening, provide the updated markdown in `redacted_base_prompt` (must preserve `# ROLE`, `## 1. INPUT PAYLOAD CONTEXT`, and `## REQUIRED JSON OUTPUT SCHEMA` 100% intact). Otherwise, return `null` for `redacted_base_prompt` so `agent_mutator.py` preserves `base_prompt` and injects `consolidated_invariant`.

system_prompt:
# ROLE: Seed Writer — Academic & Technical Thesis Author (Layer 2 — `building` Domain)

You are the primary scientific and technical writer (`seed_writer`) in the **Artificial-Degree-Printer**.
You author and revise high-quality academic degree theses (inżynierskie, magisterskie) and scientific papers in LaTeX (`thesis.tex`) or Markdown (`thesis.md`).

---

## 1. ACADEMIC CHAPTER REQUIREMENTS
Author requested sections matching the standard 6-chapter thesis canon:
- **Ch 1 (Wstęp & Cel)**: Problem motivation, formal thesis statement (*teza*), measurable goals, scope boundaries.
- **Ch 2 (SOTA & Related Work)**: Methodological taxonomy using verified citations (`\cite{...}`), clear research gap.
- **Ch 3 (Architektura)**: Component decomposition, interfaces, data flows, and **inline TikZ** or **Mermaid** diagrams.
- **Ch 4 (Implementacja)**: Algorithmic realization, core classes/functions cross-referenced via `\ref_ast{file:symbol}`.
- **Ch 5 (Eksperymenty)**: Baseline vs. Proposed comparison, ablation studies, vector plots, and tables via `\ref_csv{file:column}`.
- **Ch 6 (Podsumowanie)**: Formal evaluation of thesis statement validation, technical limitations, future work.

---

## 2. STRICT MANDATORY TEMPLATE USAGE (NO GENERIC ARTICLE)
You must **STRICTLY AND UNCONDITIONALLY** structure all LaTeX thesis documents around the verified template:
1. **Degree Theses (`inzynierska`, `magisterska`, `engineering`, `master`)**:
   - Template: **Politechnika Łódzka Thesis Template** (`ThesisPLodz.cls` based on Zarządzenie Nr 6/2025 Rektora Politechniki Łódzkiej).
   - Documentclass: `\documentclass[W2, polski]{ThesisPLodz}` (or specified faculty, e.g. `W1`, `W7`, `IFE`, and language `polski`/`english`).
   - Required macros: `\authorname{...}`, `\studentnumber{...}`, `\thesistitle{...}`, `\thesisshorttitle{...}`, `\degreename{...}`, `\fieldofstudy{...}`, `\department{...}`, `\supervisor{...}`, `\abstract{...}`, `\keywords{...}`, `\abstractsecondary{...}`, `\keywordssecondary{...}`.
   - Frontmatter is automatically generated by `ThesisPLodz.cls` (title page, blank page, TOC, abstracts).
   - Structural macros: `\chapter{...}`, `\symbolslist{...}`, `\abbreviationslist{...}`, `\definitionslist{...}`, `\addattachment{...}{...}`.
   - **ABSOLUTE BAN**: Never use generic `\documentclass{article}` or unformatted thesis drafts for degree theses!
2. **Scientific Papers / Articles (`paper`, `article`, `scientific_paper`)**:
   - Template: **IEEE Scientific Conference / Transaction Template** (`IEEEtran.cls`).
   - Documentclass: `\documentclass[conference]{IEEEtran}` (or `journal`).
   - Required structure: `\title{...}`, `\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{...}\IEEEauthorblockA{...}}`, `\maketitle`, `\begin{abstract}...\end{abstract}`, `\begin{IEEEkeywords}...\end{IEEEkeywords}`, `\section{...}`, `\bibliographystyle{IEEEtran}`.
   - **ABSOLUTE BAN**: Never deviate from the IEEEtran two-column conference structure for scientific papers!

---

## 2. STRICT SYMBOLIC & HYPERGRAPH GROUNDING (ZERO HALLUCINATIONS)
1. **Diagrams, Plots & Formula Layout (NEVER Overflow Boundaries)**:
   - **Compact TikZ Architecture Schematics**: Draw inline using **TikZ** (`\begin{tikzpicture}...\end{tikzpicture}`) in LaTeX or **Mermaid** in Markdown. **NEVER** write `\ref_fig{figures/system_architecture.pdf}` or invent unverified files! Design TikZ diagrams compactly with vertical pipelines or tiered layouts (total diagram width $\le 6.5\,\text{cm}$, node `minimum width` 4.0--5.0 cm, `node distance` 1.0--1.2 cm) so they fit naturally within a single IEEE column ($8.89\,\text{cm}$) or thesis margins without clipping.
   - **Empirical Plots**: Only reference existing figures from the hypergraph state (e.g. `\ref_fig{figures/comparison_chart.pdf}`). In plot generation scripts, use compact figure sizes (e.g. `figsize=(4.8, 3.0)` for single plots or `figsize=(6.0, 2.8)` for two subplots) with `bbox_inches="tight"`. In LaTeX figure environments, include graphics with `[width=\columnwidth,keepaspectratio]` (for IEEE papers) or `[width=0.86\textwidth,keepaspectratio]` (for theses).
   - **Concise Mathematical Formulas**: Write clean, standard, concise mathematical formulations without artificial component bloat. If a formula exceeds column width, split it cleanly across lines using `\begin{split}...\end{split}` inside `\begin{equation}` or `\begin{align}`, preventing any `Overfull \hbox` overflow.
2. **Deterministic Symbolic Pointers**:
   - Code constants/hyperparameters: `\ref_ast{file:symbol}` (e.g. `\ref_ast{config.py:LEARNING_RATE}`).
   - Empirical metrics: `\ref_csv{file:row_method:column}` or `\ref_csv{file:column}` (e.g. `\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:final_accuracy}`). Never invent column names.
   - **ABSOLUTE BAN ON MATH MODE FOR POINTERS**: NEVER enclose symbolic references in dollar signs (e.g. NEVER `$\ref_csv{...}$` or `$\ref_ast{...}$`). Write in plain text: `uzyskując dokładność \ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:final_accuracy}`.

The protocol involves:\n\\begin{enumerate}\n    \\item Generating random grid maps of size defined by \\ref_ast{config.py:GRID_SIZE} with obstacle density specified by \\ref_ast{config.py:OBSTACLE_DENSITY}.\n    \\item Running both Dijkstra and Weighted A* across \\ref_ast{config.py:TRIALS} independent trials for statistical significance.\n    \\item Recording four key metrics in \\ref_csv{results.csv}:\n    \\begin{itemize}\n        \\item $\\text{avg\\_expanded\\_nodes}$: Mean number of nodes popped from the priority queue.\n        \\item $\\text{path\\_optimality}$: Ratio of found path cost to optimal Dijkstra path cost ($L_{found} / L_{optimal}$).\n        \\item $\\text{speedup\\_factor}$: Relative reduction in execution time compared to Dijkstra.\n        \\item $\\text{success\\_rate}$: Percentage of trials yielding a valid path (1.0 for connected grids).\n    \\end{itemize}\n\\end{enumerate}\n\nThis deterministic evaluation allows for a direct comparison of the algorithmic complexity and solution quality, isolating the effect of the heuristic weighting from random graph topology variations.\n\n## Analiza Stanu Wiedzy (SOTA) oraz Propozycja Metodologiczna\n## Analiza Stanu Wiedzy (SOTA)\n\\subsection{Stan Wiedzy w Algorytmach Pathfindingu na Grafach (SOTA 2023--2025)}\n\nWspółczesna literatura poświęcona wyszukiwaniu ścieżek na siatkach (grid-based pathfinding) koncentruje się na kompromisie między optymalnością a szybkością konwergencji, szczególnie w kontekście aplikacji wymagających real-time response. Klasyczny algorytm Dijkstry \\cite{dijkstra1959note}, będący przypadkiem ogólnym BFS dla ważonych grafów, gwarantuje znalezienie ścieżki optymalnej kosztem eksploracji \\(O(E + V \\log V)\\) węzłów. Jednakże, jak wykazano w pracach benchmarkowych \\cite{sturtevant2023benchmarks}, jego brak heurystyki prowadzi do nadmiernej ekspansji węzłów w porównaniu do metod kierowanych.\n\nWprowadzenie przez Harta et al. \\cite{hart1968formal} algorytmu A* z admissible heuristic (np. odległość Manhattan lub Octile) rozwiązuje problem nadmiernej ekspansji, zapewniając optymalność przy minimalizacji liczby odwiedzonych węzłów. Jednak w praktycznych zastosowaniach robotyki i gier wideo, sztywna gwarancja optymalności bywa niewydajna czasowo. W odpowiedzi, niedawne prace \\cite{felner2024weighted, goldenberg2024suboptimal} szczegółowo analizują wariant Weighted A* (WA*), wprowadzając wagę \\(w > 1\\) do funkcji oceny \\(f(n) = g(n) + w \\cdot h(n)\\). Prace te z 2024 roku definiują ścisłe granice deoptimality (\\(\\epsilon\\)-suboptimality) wynikające ze wzrostu \\(w\\), pokazując, że przyrost szybkości jest logarytmiczny w stosunku do spadku dokładności.\n\nW zakresie heurystyk, Harabor et al. \\cite{harabor2023octile} zidentyfikowali kluczowy problem symetrii w siatkach 8-połączonych (octile grid), prowadzący do eksplozji płaskich równoważnych ścieżek. Sugerują oni łamanie symetrii poprzez priorytetyzację ruchów po ukosie, co drastycznie redukuje liczbę ekspandowanych węzłów bez utraty optymalności. Z kolei w kontekście uczenia maszynowego, Agostinelli i in. \\cite{agostinelli2024learned} demonstrują, że choć Network-Driven Heuristics (np. ViT-A*) mogą przewyższyć klasyczne metryki geometryczne w specyficznych topologiach, ich narzut obliczeniowy na wnioskowanie czyni je mniej efektywnymi niż dobrze dobrana stała waga heurystyki dla prostych siatek o umiarkowanej wielkości.\n\nOstatnie kierunki badań \\cite{chen2024focal, shperberg2024deadline} skupiają się na adaptacyjnych wagach heurystyki, które zmieniają się dynamicznie w zależności od głębokości przeszukiwania lub zbliżania się do celu. Mimo to, większość tych systemów wymaga zaawansowanej infrastruktury. Istnieje więc luka badawcza w prostych, deterministycznych implementacjach Weighted Octile A*, które umożliwiają precyzyjną kontrolę nad kompromisem czasowym (speedup) a optymalnością ścieżki przy użyciu statycznej, ale dobrze uzasadnionej wagi \\(w\\), co jest kluczowe dla systemów wbudowanych o ograniczonych zasobach \\cite{zhang2025hardware}. Niniejsza praca adresuje tę lukę poprzez empiryczną evaluację wpływu parametru \\(w\\) na metryki wydajności w kontrolowanym środowisku symulacyjnym.\n\n## Section II: Related Work\n\\section{Related Work}\n\\label{sec:related_work}\n\nThe evolution of graph-based pathfinding algorithms has transitioned from uninformed, distance-optimality guarantees to heuristic-driven efficiency, particularly in real-time applications such as robotics and gaming. This section reviews the theoretical foundations of Dijkstra's algorithm, A* search, Weighted A*, and recent advancements in symmetry breaking and heuristic dominance.\n\n\\subsection{Uninformed Search: Dijkstra's Algorithm}\nDijkstra's algorithm \\cite{dijkstra1959note} remains the gold standard for finding shortest paths in graphs with non-negative edge weights. By expanding nodes in order of increasing path cost from the source, it guarantees optimality ($g(n)$ minimization). However, its uninformed nature leads to $O(V^2)$ or $O(E + V \\log V)$ time complexity depending on the implementation, resulting in excessive node expansion ($\\text{avg\\_expanded\\_nodes}$) even when the goal is nearby. In dense grid environments defined by parameters such as \\ref_ast{config.py:GRID_SIZE} and obstacle density \\ref_ast{config.py:OBSTACLE_DENSITY}, this inefficiency becomes a critical bottleneck for real-time systems.\n\n\\subsection{Heuristic Search: A* and Optimality}\nTo address Dijkstra's limitations, Hart, Nilsson, and Raphael introduced the A* algorithm \\cite{hart1968formal}, which incorporates a heuristic function $h(n)$ to guide search toward the goal. When $h(n)$ is admissible (never overestimates the true cost), A* guarantees optimal path length ($\\text{path\\_optimality} = 1$). For grid-based maps, common heuristics include Manhattan distance and Octile distance, which accounts for diagonal movement costs in 8-connected grids \\cite{sturtevant2012benchmarks}. While A* significantly reduces expanded nodes compared to Dijkstra, its strict admissibility requirement often results in slower convergence than necessary for applications where near-optimal solutions are acceptable.\n\n\\subsection{Weighted A*: Trading Optimality for Speed}\nThe Weighted A* (WA*) algorithm \\cite{pohl1970heuristic} modifies the evaluation function to $f(n) = g(n) + w \\cdot h(n)$, where $w > 1$. This prioritization accelerates search convergence by biasing the exploration toward the goal. As established in theoretical bounds \\cite{pearl1984heuristics}, WA* with weight $w$ guarantees a solution within a factor of $(2 - 1/w)$ of the optimal path length. Recent studies \\cite{felner2024weighted, goldenberg2024suboptimal} demonstrate that increasing $w$ yields logarithmic speedups in execution time but introduces predictable suboptimality. The parameter \\ref_ast{config.py:WEIGHT_A_STAR} controls this trade-off, allowing practitioners to balance the `speedup_factor` against the acceptable loss in `path_optimality`.\n\n\\subsection{Symmetry Breaking and Modern Heuristics}\nIn grid environments, multiple equally optimal paths often exist between source and goal, leading to symmetric expansions that bloat search trees. Harabor et al. \\cite{harabor2011online} proposed Jump Point Search (JPS) to prune these symmetries during exploration. More recently, \\cite{harabor2023heuristic} highlighted the importance of tie-breaking rules in Octile heuristics to further reduce node expansion. Concurrently, machine learning approaches \\cite{agostinelli2024learned} have attempted to learn heuristic weights dynamically, though their computational overhead often limits applicability compared to static weighted methods for simple grid topologies.\n\n\\subsection{Research Gap}\nWhile individual components (Weighted A*, Octile heuristics) are well-understood, there is a need for rigorous empirical analysis of the sensitivity of \\ref_ast{config.py:WEIGHT_A_STAR} on standard metrics like \\ref_csv{results.csv:baseline:avg_expanded_nodes} versus \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:speedup_factor}. This work bridges that gap by implementing a robust Weighted Octile A* and quantifying its performance boundaries against the Dijkstra baseline.\n\n## Section III: Proposed Methodology\n\\section{Proposed Methodology}\n\\label{sec:methodology}\n\nThe proposed approach evolves the baseline uninformed search into a heuristic-driven Weighted A* algorithm tailored for 8-connected grid environments. This section formalizes the mathematical definition of the Octile heuristic, describes the integration of the weighting factor \\(w\\), and details the evaluation protocol used to quantify the trade-off between computational efficiency and path optimality.\n\n\\subsection{Octile Heuristic Formulation}\nTo accurately estimate the cost-to-go in an 8-connected grid (allowing horizontal, vertical, and diagonal movements), we utilize the Octile distance heuristic \\(h(n)\\). Unlike the Manhattan distance, which restricts movement to cardinal directions, or Euclidean distance, which involves computationally expensive square roots, the Octile heuristic accounts for the geometry of diagonal moves with cost $\\sqrt{2}$ (approximately 1.414) relative to the cardinal cost of 1.\n\nGiven a current node \\(n\\) at coordinates $(x, y)$ and a goal node at $(x_g, y_g)$, the heuristic is defined as:\n\\begin{equation}\n    h(n) = d_{min} + (\\sqrt{2} - 1) \\cdot d_{max}\n\\end{equation}\nwhere $d_{min} = |x - x_g|$ and $d_{max} = \\max(|y - y_g|, |x - x_g|)$ represent the minimum and maximum coordinate differences, respectively. This formulation ensures consistency (monotonicity) for grid graphs with non-negative edge weights, a prerequisite for optimal pathfinding in standard A*. However, as discussed in Section II, strict admissibility ($w=1$) often results in excessive node expansion. Therefore, we introduce the heuristic weight \\(w\\), controlled by the constant \\ref_ast{config.py:WEIGHT_A_STAR}, to bias the search.\n\n\\subsection{Weighted A* Implementation}\nThe core modification lies in the evaluation function $f(n)$ used by the priority queue in \\ref_ast{core.py:a_star_search}. While the baseline Dijkstra algorithm corresponds to $h(n)=0$ (or effectively $w=0$), standard A* uses $w=1$. Our proposed method implements Weighted A* (WA*) as follows:\n\\begin{equation}\n    f(n) = g(n) + w \\cdot h_{octile}(n)\n\\end{equation}\nwhere $g(n)$ is the actual cost from the start node to $n$, and $w > 1$ is a user-defined scalar constant. In our implementation, this weight is read directly from \\ref_ast{config.py:WEIGHT_A_STAR}. \n\nWhen $w$ increases, the heuristic term dominates the evaluation function, causing the algorithm to behave more like Greedy Best-First Search. This aggressively prioritizes nodes closer to the goal (in terms of Octile distance), thereby reducing the number of explored states. Conversely, as $w \\to 0$, the algorithm approaches Dijkstra's behavior, expanding nodes uniformly in all directions until the goal is found.\n\n\\subsection{Evaluation Protocol and Metrics}\nTo empirically validate the impact of \\ref_ast{config.py:WEIGHT_A_STAR} on performance, we implemented a simulation loop in \\ref_ast{core.py:train_and_evaluate}. The protocol involves:\n\\begin{enumerate}\n    \\item Generating random grid maps of size defined by \\ref_ast{config.py:GRID_SIZE} with obstacle density specified by \\ref_ast{config.py:OBSTACLE_DENSITY}.\n    \\item Running both Dijkstra and Weighted A* across \\ref_ast{config.py:TRIALS} independent trials for statistical significance.\n    \\item Recording four key metrics in \\ref_csv{results.csv}:\n    \\begin{itemize}\n        \\item $\\text{avg\\_expanded\\_nodes}$: Mean number of nodes popped from the priority queue.\n        \\item $\\text{path\\_optimality}$: Ratio of found path cost to optimal Dijkstra path cost ($L_{found} / L_{optimal}$).\n        \\item $\\text{speedup\\_factor}$: Relative reduction in execution time compared to Dijkstra.\n        \\item $\\text{success\\_rate}$: Percentage of trials yielding a valid path (1.0 for connected grids).\n    \\end{itemize}\n\\end{enumerate}\n\nThis deterministic evaluation allows for a direct comparison of the algorithmic complexity and solution quality, isolating the effect of the heuristic weighting from random graph topology variations.\n\n## Poprawki strukturalne i walidacja wskaźników symboliki w thesis.md\n\\subsection{Korekta dokumentacji technicznej i walidacja referencji}\\label{sec:corrections}\n\nW procesie ewolucji projektu (Task \\texttt{T5\\_FIX\\_2}) dokonano korekty pliku \\texttt{thesis.md} w celu usunięcia niepoprawnych odwołań do metrik oraz dostosowania nazewnictwa stałych konfiguracyjnych do aktualnej struktury źródłowej. \n\nPo pierwsze, zweryfikowano integralność referencji CSV. The objective is to quantify the trade-off between computational efficiency (measured by \\texttt{speedup\\_factor} and \\texttt{avg\\_expanded\\_nodes}) and path optimality ($L_{found}/L_{optimal}$). Source and goal nodes are uniformly sampled from free cells. The baseline Dijkstra algorithm serves as the reference for optimal path cost ($L_{optimal}$). The results validate the utility of \\ref_ast{config.py:HEURISTIC_WEIGHT} as a tunable parameter to balance these competing demands.\n\n## Section V: Conclusion\n\\section{Conclusion}\\label{sec:conclusion}\n\n\\subsection{Validation of Research Objectives}\nThis paper addressed the research gap regarding deterministic, lightweight implementations of Weighted Octile A* for grid-based pathfinding. Niniejsza praca adresuje tę lukę poprzez empiryczną evaluację wpływu parametru \\(w\\) na metryki wydajności w kontrolowanym środowisku symulacyjnym.\n\n## Section II: Related Work\n\\section{Related Work}\n\\label{sec:related_work}\n\nThe evolution of graph-based pathfinding algorithms has transitioned from uninformed, distance-optimality guarantees to heuristic-driven efficiency, particularly in real-time applications such as robotics and gaming. This section reviews the theoretical foundations of Dijkstra's algorithm, A* search, Weighted A*, and recent advancements in symmetry breaking and heuristic dominance.\n\n\\subsection{Uninformed Search: Dijkstra's Algorithm}\nDijkstra's algorithm \\cite{dijkstra1959note} remains the gold standard for finding shortest paths in graphs with non-negative edge weights. By expanding nodes in order of increasing path cost from the source, it guarantees optimality ($g(n)$ minimization). However, its uninformed nature leads to $O(V^2)$ or $O(E + V \\log V)$ time complexity depending on the implementation, resulting in excessive node expansion ($\\text{avg\\_expanded\\_nodes}$) even when the goal is nearby. In dense grid environments defined by parameters such as \\ref_ast{config.py:GRID_SIZE} and obstacle density \\ref_ast{config.py:OBSTACLE_DENSITY}, this inefficiency becomes a critical bottleneck for real-time systems.\n\n\\subsection{Heuristic Search: A* and Optimality}\nTo address Dijkstra's limitations, Hart, Nilsson, and Raphael introduced the A* algorithm \\cite{hart1968formal}, which incorporates a heuristic function $h(n)$ to guide search toward the goal. When $h(n)$ is admissible (never overestimates the true cost), A* guarantees optimal path length ($\\text{path\\_optimality} = 1$). For grid-based maps, common heuristics include Manhattan distance and Octile distance, which accounts for diagonal movement costs in 8-connected grids \\cite{sturtevant2012benchmarks}. While A* significantly reduces expanded nodes compared to Dijkstra, its strict admissibility requirement often results in slower convergence than necessary for applications where near-optimal solutions are acceptable.\n\n\\subsection{Weighted A*: Trading Optimality for Speed}\nThe Weighted A* (WA*) algorithm \\cite{pohl1970heuristic} modifies the evaluation function to $f(n) = g(n) + w \\cdot h(n)$, where $w > 1$. This prioritization accelerates search convergence by biasing the exploration toward the goal. As established in theoretical bounds \\cite{pearl1984heuristics}, WA* with weight $w$ guarantees a solution within a factor of $(2 - 1/w)$ of the optimal path length. Recent studies \\cite{felner2024weighted, goldenberg2024suboptimal} demonstrate that increasing $w$ yields logarithmic speedups in execution time but introduces predictable suboptimality. The parameter \\ref_ast{config.py:WEIGHT_A_STAR} controls this trade-off, allowing practitioners to balance the `speedup_factor` against the acceptable loss in `path_optimality`.\n\n\\subsection{Symmetry Breaking and Modern Heuristics}\nIn grid environments, multiple equally optimal paths often exist between source and goal, leading to symmetric expansions that bloat search trees. Harabor et al. \\cite{harabor2011online} proposed Jump Point Search (JPS) to prune these symmetries during exploration. More recently, \\cite{harabor2023heuristic} highlighted the importance of tie-breaking rules in Octile heuristics to further reduce node expansion. Concurrently, machine learning approaches \\cite{agostinelli2024learned} have attempted to learn heuristic weights dynamically, though their computational overhead often limits applicability compared to static weighted methods for simple grid topologies.\n\n\\subsection{Research Gap}\nWhile individual components (Weighted A*, Octile heuristics) are well-understood, there is a need for rigorous empirical analysis of the sensitivity of \\ref_ast{config.py:WEIGHT_A_STAR} on standard metrics like \\ref_csv{results.csv:baseline:avg_expanded_nodes} versus \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:speedup_factor}. This work bridges that gap by implementing a robust Weighted Octile A* and quantifying its performance boundaries against the Dijkstra baseline.\n\n## Section III: Proposed Methodology\n\\section{Proposed Methodology}\n\\label{sec:methodology}\n\nThe proposed approach evolves the baseline uninformed search into a heuristic-driven Weighted A* algorithm tailored for 8-connected grid environments. This section formalizes the mathematical definition of the Octile heuristic, describes the integration of the weighting factor \\(w\\), and details the evaluation protocol used to quantify the trade-off between computational efficiency and path optimality.\n\n\\subsection{Octile Heuristic Formulation}\nTo accurately estimate the cost-to-go in an 8-connected grid (allowing horizontal, vertical, and diagonal movements), we utilize the Octile distance heuristic \\(h(n)\\). Unlike the Manhattan distance, which restricts movement to cardinal directions, or Euclidean distance, which involves computationally expensive square roots, the Octile heuristic accounts for the geometry of diagonal moves with cost $\\sqrt{2}$ (approximately 1.414) relative to the cardinal cost of 1.\n\nGiven a current node \\(n\\) at coordinates $(x, y)$ and a goal node at $(x_g, y_g)$, the heuristic is defined as:\n\\begin{equation}\n    h(n) = d_{min} + (\\sqrt{2} - 1) \\cdot d_{max}\n\\end{equation}\nwhere $d_{min} = |x - x_g|$ and $d_{max} = \\max(|y - y_g|, |x - x_g|)$ represent the minimum and maximum coordinate differences, respectively. This formulation ensures consistency (monotonicity) for grid graphs with non-negative edge weights, a prerequisite for optimal pathfinding in standard A*. However, as discussed in Section II, strict admissibility ($w=1$) often results in excessive node expansion. Therefore, we introduce the heuristic weight \\(w\\), controlled by the constant \\ref_ast{config.py:WEIGHT_A_STAR}, to bias the search.\n\n\\subsection{Weighted A* Implementation}\nThe core modification lies in the evaluation function $f(n)$ used by the priority queue in \\ref_ast{core.py:a_star_search}. While the baseline Dijkstra algorithm corresponds to $h(n)=0$ (or effectively $w=0$), standard A* uses $w=1$. Our proposed method implements Weighted A* (WA*) as follows:\n\\begin{equation}\n    f(n) = g(n) + w \\cdot h_{octile}(n)\n\\end{equation}\nwhere $g(n)$ is the actual cost from the start node to $n$, and $w > 1$ is a user-defined scalar constant. In our implementation, this weight is read directly from \\ref_ast{config.py:WEIGHT_A_STAR}. \n\nWhen $w$ increases, the heuristic term dominates the evaluation function, causing the algorithm to behave more like Greedy Best-First Search. This aggressively prioritizes nodes closer to the goal (in terms of Octile distance), thereby reducing the number of explored states. Conversely, as $w \\to 0$, the algorithm approaches Dijkstra's behavior, expanding nodes uniformly in all directions until the goal is found.\n\n\\subsection{Evaluation Protocol and Metrics}\nTo empirically validate the impact of \\ref_ast{config.py:WEIGHT_A_STAR} on performance, we implemented a simulation loop in \\ref_ast{core.py:train_and_evaluate}. The protocol involves:\n\\begin{enumerate}\n    \\item Generating random grid maps of size defined by \\ref_ast{config.py:GRID_SIZE} with obstacle density specified by \\ref_ast{config.py:OBSTACLE_DENSITY}.\n    \\item Running both Dijkstra and Weighted A* across \\ref_ast{config.py:TRIALS} independent trials for statistical significance.\n    \\item Recording four key metrics in \\ref_csv{results.csv}:\n    \\begin{itemize}\n        \\item $\\text{avg\\_expanded\\_nodes}$: Mean number of nodes popped from the priority queue.\n        \\item $\\text{path\\_optimality}$: Ratio of found path cost to optimal Dijkstra path cost ($L_{found} / L_{optimal}$).\n        \\item $\\text{speedup\\_factor}$: Relative reduction in execution time compared to Dijkstra.\n        \\item $\\text{success\\_rate}$: Percentage of trials yielding a valid path (1.0 for connected grids).\n    \\end{itemize}\n\\end{enumerate}\n\nThis deterministic evaluation allows for a direct comparison of the algorithmic complexity and solution quality, isolating the effect of the heuristic weighting from random graph topology variations.\n\n## Poprawki strukturalne i walidacja wskaźników symboliki w thesis.md\n\\subsection{Korekta dokumentacji technicznej i walidacja referencji}\\label{sec:corrections}\n\nW procesie ewolucji projektu (Task \\texttt{T5\\_FIX\\_2}) dokonano korekty pliku \\texttt{thesis.md} w celu usunięcia niepoprawnych odwołań do metrik oraz dostosowania nazewnictwa stałych konfiguracyjnych do aktualnej struktury źródłowej. \n\nPo pierwsze, zweryfikowano integralność referencji CSV. You are the **Evolution Architect** (`evolution_architect`) in the **Artificial-Degree-Printer (Neuro-Symbolic Harness)**.
You oversee structural adaptation, prompt evolution, tool synthesis, and Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) promotor communication across 3 formal gates (Gate 1: Scope, Gate 2: Methodology, Gate 3: Defense).

---

## 1. EVOLUTIONARY ACTIONS
When Layer 3 reports a failure or Layer 1 reports a missing specialization, select exactly one decision:
- **`MUTATE_AGENT`**: For preventable agent mistakes, inject a crisp rule into `## LEARNED RULES AND CONSTRAINTS` (GUARDS are immutable).
- **`CREATE_AGENT`**: When a specialized domain capability is missing (e.g. `"anomaly_ml_specialist"`, `"diagram_architect"`).
- **`SPLIT_AGENT`**: When an agent repeatedly fails due to overloaded scope (e.g. split `seed_tester` into `unit_tester` + `benchmark_runner`).
- **`CREATE_TOOL`**: When a recurring verification error can be validated deterministically by a synthesized Python script.
- **`HITL`**: For Gate 1/2/3 promotor checkpoints or contradictory user requirements.

---

## 2. MANDATORY SCHEMA RULES
1. The action key MUST be `"decision"`. (DO NOT use `"action"`, `"status"`, or `"response"`).
2. The agent identifier MUST be `"agent_id"` and MUST MATCH `"failed_agent"` from the payload (never default to `seed_coder` if another agent failed).
3. The injected constraint MUST be `"rule"`.
4. Output strictly a single raw JSON object without conversational text.

---

### MUTATE_AGENT (Inject learned rule into failed agent):
```json
{
  "decision": "MUTATE_AGENT",
  "agent_id": "seed_coder",

}

  "specialization": "anomaly_ml_specialist",

}

Niniejsza praca adresuje tę lukę poprzez empiryczną evaluację wpływu parametru \\(w\\) na metryki wydajności w kontrolowanym środowisku symulacyjnym.\n\n## Section II: Related Work\n\\section{Related Work}\n\\label{sec:related_work}\n\nThe evolution of graph-based pathfinding algorithms has transitioned from uninformed, distance-optimality guarantees to heuristic-driven efficiency, particularly in real-time applications such as robotics and gaming. This section reviews the theoretical foundations of Dijkstra's algorithm, A* search, Weighted A*, and recent advancements in symmetry breaking and heuristic dominance.\n\n\\subsection{Uninformed Search: Dijkstra's Algorithm}\nDijkstra's algorithm \\cite{dijkstra1959note} remains the gold standard for finding shortest paths in graphs with non-negative edge weights. By expanding nodes in order of increasing path cost from the source, it guarantees optimality ($g(n)$ minimization). However, its uninformed nature leads to $O(V^2)$ or $O(E + V \\log V)$ time complexity depending on the implementation, resulting in excessive node expansion ($\\text{avg\\_expanded\\_nodes}$) even when the goal is nearby. In dense grid environments defined by parameters such as \\ref_ast{config.py:GRID_SIZE} and obstacle density \\ref_ast{config.py:OBSTACLE_DENSITY}, this inefficiency becomes a critical bottleneck for real-time systems.\n\n\\subsection{Heuristic Search: A* and Optimality}\nTo address Dijkstra's limitations, Hart, Nilsson, and Raphael introduced the A* algorithm \\cite{hart1968formal}, which incorporates a heuristic function $h(n)$ to guide search toward the goal. When $h(n)$ is admissible (never overestimates the true cost), A* guarantees optimal path length ($\\text{path\\_optimality} = 1$). For grid-based maps, common heuristics include Manhattan distance and Octile distance, which accounts for diagonal movement costs in 8-connected grids \\cite{sturtevant2012benchmarks}. While A* significantly reduces expanded nodes compared to Dijkstra, its strict admissibility requirement often results in slower convergence than necessary for applications where near-optimal solutions are acceptable.\n\n\\subsection{Weighted A*: Trading Optimality for Speed}\nThe Weighted A* (WA*) algorithm \\cite{pohl1970heuristic} modifies the evaluation function to $f(n) = g(n) + w \\cdot h(n)$, where $w > 1$. This prioritization accelerates search convergence by biasing the exploration toward the goal. As established in theoretical bounds \\cite{pearl1984heuristics}, WA* with weight $w$ guarantees a solution within a factor of $(2 - 1/w)$ of the optimal path length. Recent studies \\cite{felner2024weighted, goldenberg2024suboptimal} demonstrate that increasing $w$ yields logarithmic speedups in execution time but introduces predictable suboptimality. The parameter \\ref_ast{config.py:WEIGHT_A_STAR} controls this trade-off, allowing practitioners to balance the `speedup_factor` against the acceptable loss in `path_optimality`.\n\n\\subsection{Symmetry Breaking and Modern Heuristics}\nIn grid environments, multiple equally optimal paths often exist between source and goal, leading to symmetric expansions that bloat search trees. Harabor et al. \\cite{harabor2011online} proposed Jump Point Search (JPS) to prune these symmetries during exploration. More recently, \\cite{harabor2023heuristic} highlighted the importance of tie-breaking rules in Octile heuristics to further reduce node expansion. Concurrently, machine learning approaches \\cite{agostinelli2024learned} have attempted to learn heuristic weights dynamically, though their computational overhead often limits applicability compared to static weighted methods for simple grid topologies.\n\n\\subsection{Research Gap}\nWhile individual components (Weighted A*, Octile heuristics) are well-understood, there is a need for rigorous empirical analysis of the sensitivity of \\ref_ast{config.py:WEIGHT_A_STAR} on standard metrics like \\ref_csv{results.csv:baseline:avg_expanded_nodes} versus \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:speedup_factor}. This work bridges that gap by implementing a robust Weighted Octile A* and quantifying its performance boundaries against the Dijkstra baseline.\n\n## Section III: Proposed Methodology\n\\section{Proposed Methodology}\n\\label{sec:methodology}\n\nThe proposed approach evolves the baseline uninformed search into a heuristic-driven Weighted A* algorithm tailored for 8-connected grid environments. This section formalizes the mathematical definition of the Octile heuristic, describes the integration of the weighting factor \\(w\\), and details the evaluation protocol used to quantify the trade-off between computational efficiency and path optimality.\n\n\\subsection{Octile Heuristic Formulation}\nTo accurately estimate the cost-to-go in an 8-connected grid (allowing horizontal, vertical, and diagonal movements), we utilize the Octile distance heuristic \\(h(n)\\). Unlike the Manhattan distance, which restricts movement to cardinal directions, or Euclidean distance, which involves computationally expensive square roots, the Octile heuristic accounts for the geometry of diagonal moves with cost $\\sqrt{2}$ (approximately 1.414) relative to the cardinal cost of 1.\n\nGiven a current node \\(n\\) at coordinates $(x, y)$ and a goal node at $(x_g, y_g)$, the heuristic is defined as:\n\\begin{equation}\n    h(n) = d_{min} + (\\sqrt{2} - 1) \\cdot d_{max}\n\\end{equation}\nwhere $d_{min} = |x - x_g|$ and $d_{max} = \\max(|y - y_g|, |x - x_g|)$ represent the minimum and maximum coordinate differences, respectively. This formulation ensures consistency (monotonicity) for grid graphs with non-negative edge weights, a prerequisite for optimal pathfinding in standard A*. In our implementation, this weight is read directly from \\ref_ast{config.py:WEIGHT_A_STAR}. \n\nWhen $w$ increases, the heuristic term dominates the evaluation function, causing the algorithm to behave more like Greedy Best-First Search. This aggressively prioritizes nodes closer to the goal (in terms of Octile distance), thereby reducing the number of explored states. You are the **Evolution Architect** (`evolution_architect`) in the **Artificial-Degree-Printer (Neuro-Symbolic Harness)**.
You oversee structural adaptation, prompt evolution, tool synthesis, and Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) promotor communication across 3 formal gates (Gate 1: Scope, Gate 2: Methodology, Gate 3: Defense).

---

## 1. EVOLUTIONARY ACTIONS
When Layer 3 reports a failure or Layer 1 reports a missing specialization, select exactly one decision:
- **`MUTATE_AGENT`**: For preventable agent mistakes, inject a crisp rule into `## LEARNED RULES AND CONSTRAINTS` (GUARDS are immutable).
- **`CREATE_AGENT`**: When a specialized domain capability is missing (e.g. `"anomaly_ml_specialist"`, `"diagram_architect"`).
- **`SPLIT_AGENT`**: When an agent repeatedly fails due to overloaded scope (e.g. split `seed_tester` into `unit_tester` + `benchmark_runner`).
- **`CREATE_TOOL`**: When a recurring verification error can be validated deterministically by a synthesized Python script.
- **`HITL`**: For Gate 1/2/3 promotor checkpoints or contradictory user requirements.

---

## 2. MANDATORY SCHEMA RULES
1. The action key MUST be `"decision"`. (DO NOT use `"action"`, `"status"`, or `"response"`).
2. The agent identifier MUST be `"agent_id"` and MUST MATCH `"failed_agent"` from the payload (never default to `seed_coder` if another agent failed).
3. The injected constraint MUST be `"rule"`.
4. Output strictly a single raw JSON object without conversational text.

---

## 3. REQUIRED JSON SCHEMAS BY DECISION

### MUTATE_AGENT (Inject learned rule into failed agent):
```json
{
  "decision": "MUTATE_AGENT",
  "agent_id": "seed_coder",
  "rule": "Always preserve strict AST, CSV and symbolic reference parity across generated artifacts.",
  "rationale": "Enforcing signature parity prevents contract mismatches detected in task T1."
}
```

```json
{
  "decision": "CREATE_AGENT",
  "specialization": "anomaly_ml_specialist",
  "domain": "building",
  "rationale": "Task requires specialized ML validation not covered by general seed agents."
}

```json

  "decision": "CREATE_TOOL",
  "tool_name": "ast_signature_validator.py",
  "tool_code": "import sys, ast\n# deterministic validator\nsys.exit(0)",
  "rationale": "Synthesized deterministic AST parity validator to prevent repeated syntax regressions."
}

  "hitl_gate": "GATE_1_OUTLINE_APPROVAL",

system_prompt:
# ROLE: Seed Writer — Academic & Technical Thesis Author (Layer 2 — `building` Domain)

You are the primary scientific and technical writer (`seed_writer`) in the **Artificial-Degree-Printer**.
You author and revise high-quality academic degree theses (inżynierskie, magisterskie) and scientific papers in LaTeX (`thesis.tex`) or Markdown (`thesis.md`).

---

## 1. ACADEMIC CHAPTER REQUIREMENTS
Author requested sections matching the standard 6-chapter thesis canon:
- **Ch 1 (Wstęp & Cel)**: Problem motivation, formal thesis statement (*teza*), measurable goals, scope boundaries.
- **Ch 2 (SOTA & Related Work)**: Methodological taxonomy using verified citations (`\cite{...}`), clear research gap.
- **Ch 3 (Architektura)**: Component decomposition, interfaces, data flows, and **inline TikZ** or **Mermaid** diagrams.
- **Ch 4 (Implementacja)**: Algorithmic realization, core classes/functions cross-referenced via `\ref_ast{file:symbol}`.
- **Ch 5 (Eksperymenty)**: Baseline vs. Proposed comparison, ablation studies, vector plots, and tables via `\ref_csv{file:column}`.
- **Ch 6 (Podsumowanie)**: Formal evaluation of thesis statement validation, technical limitations, future work.

---

## 2. STRICT MANDATORY TEMPLATE USAGE (NO GENERIC ARTICLE)
You must **STRICTLY AND UNCONDITIONALLY** structure all LaTeX thesis documents around the verified template:
1. **Degree Theses (`inzynierska`, `magisterska`, `engineering`, `master`)**:
   - Template: **Politechnika Łódzka Thesis Template** (`ThesisPLodz.cls` based on Zarządzenie Nr 6/2025 Rektora Politechniki Łódzkiej).
   - Documentclass: `\documentclass[W2, polski]{ThesisPLodz}` (or specified faculty, e.g. `W1`, `W7`, `IFE`, and language `polski`/`english`).
   - Required macros: `\authorname{...}`, `\studentnumber{...}`, `\thesistitle{...}`, `\thesisshorttitle{...}`, `\degreename{...}`, `\fieldofstudy{...}`, `\department{...}`, `\supervisor{...}`, `\abstract{...}`, `\keywords{...}`, `\abstractsecondary{...}`, `\keywordssecondary{...}`.
   - Frontmatter is automatically generated by `ThesisPLodz.cls` (title page, blank page, TOC, abstracts).
   - Structural macros: `\chapter{...}`, `\symbolslist{...}`, `\abbreviationslist{...}`, `\definitionslist{...}`, `\addattachment{...}{...}`.
   - **ABSOLUTE BAN**: Never use generic `\documentclass{article}` or unformatted thesis drafts for degree theses!
2. **Scientific Papers / Articles (`paper`, `article`, `scientific_paper`)**:
   - Template: **IEEE Scientific Conference / Transaction Template** (`IEEEtran.cls`).
   - Documentclass: `\documentclass[conference]{IEEEtran}` (or `journal`).
   - Required structure: `\title{...}`, `\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{...}\IEEEauthorblockA{...}}`, `\maketitle`, `\begin{abstract}...\end{abstract}`, `\begin{IEEEkeywords}...\end{IEEEkeywords}`, `\section{...}`, `\bibliographystyle{IEEEtran}`.
   - **ABSOLUTE BAN**: Never deviate from the IEEEtran two-column conference structure for scientific papers!

---

## 2. STRICT SYMBOLIC & HYPERGRAPH GROUNDING (ZERO HALLUCINATIONS)
1. **Diagrams, Plots & Formula Layout (NEVER Overflow Boundaries)**:
   - **Compact TikZ Architecture Schematics**: Draw inline using **TikZ** (`\begin{tikzpicture}...\end{tikzpicture}`) in LaTeX or **Mermaid** in Markdown. **NEVER** write `\ref_fig{figures/system_architecture.pdf}` or invent unverified files! Design TikZ diagrams compactly with vertical pipelines or tiered layouts (total diagram width $\le 6.5\,\text{cm}$, node `minimum width` 4.0--5.0 cm, `node distance` 1.0--1.2 cm) so they fit naturally within a single IEEE column ($8.89\,\text{cm}$) or thesis margins without clipping.
   - **Empirical Plots**: Only reference existing figures from the hypergraph state (e.g. `\ref_fig{figures/comparison_chart.pdf}`). In plot generation scripts, use compact figure sizes (e.g. `figsize=(4.8, 3.0)` for single plots or `figsize=(6.0, 2.8)` for two subplots) with `bbox_inches="tight"`. In LaTeX figure environments, include graphics with `[width=\columnwidth,keepaspectratio]` (for IEEE papers) or `[width=0.86\textwidth,keepaspectratio]` (for theses).
   - **Concise Mathematical Formulas**: Write clean, standard, concise mathematical formulations without artificial component bloat. If a formula exceeds column width, split it cleanly across lines using `\begin{split}...\end{split}` inside `\begin{equation}` or `\begin{align}`, preventing any `Overfull \hbox` overflow.
2. **Deterministic Symbolic Pointers**:
